extracted.intended_audience: journalism researchers, journalism educators, and newswriting instructors
extracted.subtask_description: Descriptive model of the newswriting process derived from protocol analysis of professional and student reporters, emphasizing lead-writing, recursive text production, memory/notes use, short-term planning, rereading, and editing behavior. Useful for research and for teaching newswriting methodology.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lead-writing as independent task
rubrics_metrics.description: The lead-writing task for news stories is an independent act which must be completed before the main text of the story is produced.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lead writing is an integrated task involving review of notes, memory, writing, analyzing, and revising; it concludes with the writer gaining a 'sense of purpose' or 'direction for the story.' Writers use the lead as a barometer for the remainder of the text and will revise the lead if it no longer fits the story's direction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lead determines direction, tone, and story focus
rubrics_metrics.description: The lead selection and writing process narrows down and selects a concept around which the story can be built; the lead determines what element is most important to the story.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lead-writing is often the most time-consuming part (usually taking from one-fourth to one-third of total writing time). Even if a lead idea emerges during reporting, writers still reread and analyze it to ensure it fits tone and direction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lead is not limited to 5 W&H; may involve several paragraphs
rubrics_metrics.description: Lead writing is not a matter of consciously selecting the 5 W and H, and it often involves the completion of several paragraphs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Focus of lead instruction should consider the writer's use of the lead to set direction (writer-focused), not only its reader-facing attention-getting or summary function.

rubrics_metrics.name: Text production is recursive and hierarchical (not linear)
rubrics_metrics.description: Text production is a recursive, hierarchical set of tasks rather than a simple linear plan–write–rewrite sequence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Activities are embedded and repeated; writers rarely follow a pre-established outline for the whole story but organize as they write. The process parallels composition models in recursion but is unique in its use of lead-writing and memory.

rubrics_metrics.name: Organize-as-you-write (minimal preplanning/outlining)
rubrics_metrics.description: Newswriters typically do not plan or organize their stories in advance; instead organizing a story as it is being written facilitates logical development.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Traditional prewriting outlining is less necessary; writers set short-range goals rather than an overall plan or ranking of facts in advance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Short-range goals and paragraph-level planning
rubrics_metrics.description: Writers concentrate on planning, writing, and editing two or three sentences at a time (the normal length of the news paragraph) and set short-term goals rather than goals for the entire story.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Writers do not stop to evaluate the entire story; they continually use memory, notes, analysis, planning and rereading to propel them through paragraph development.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of memory and notes for recall
rubrics_metrics.description: Memory is the writers’ most valuable tool for obtaining information during the writing process; recall is initiated through cues provided by the notes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recall of general ideas leads writers back to notes for detail; memory helps recreate mental scenes and dialogue that are then translated into text. The close link between recall and notes is apparent in protocol transcripts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Continuous rereading and internal editing
rubrics_metrics.description: Writers depend heavily on rereading and internal editing to keep on track; rereading often occurs in small chunks (one or two sentences).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rereading generates ideas for completing thoughts and keeps the writer aligned with the lead's set direction. Rereading also functions as a way for writers to view their text from a reader's point of view.

rubrics_metrics.name: Two kinds of editing: revision (meaning) and polish (style)
rubrics_metrics.description: Editing during the process occurs in two forms: editing for revision (meaning and direction) and editing for polish (spelling, style, punctuation).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editing for revision happens continually during development as writers reread, check notes and set short-term goals; editing for polish occurs during writing and in final read-throughs. Final read-through(s) check continuity and focus and may include polish.

rubrics_metrics.name: Final read-through checks continuity and focus
rubrics_metrics.description: At least one final read-through of the complete story is part of the process; the final read-through is a check for continuity and focus of the story.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Some writers reread their stories two or three times. The final read-through focuses on the story as a whole and also catches polish issues but is primarily used to confirm that the story 'works' as constructed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of previously written text to decide next steps
rubrics_metrics.description: Information already written in the story itself leads the writer to decide what should be written next—paragraph ideas spawn from previously written paragraphs or from recall.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Each paragraph topic develops from what has just been written or from memory; writers use the text itself as a cueing mechanism for subsequent development.

rubrics_metrics.name: Handling interruptions by returning to local context
rubrics_metrics.description: Interruptions do not create major problems because returning to the task involves only returning to the sentence or paragraph, not the concept for the story as a whole.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because writers maintain a sense of direction via the lead and paragraph-level goals, resuming after interruptions is localized rather than requiring re-planning of the entire piece.

rubrics_metrics.name: Audience awareness is largely implicit (writer-as-sample-reader)
rubrics_metrics.description: Writers rarely verbalize thoughts about the audience; many use themselves as a sample audience—'If I can understand it, then I know my readers can.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Student writers more often verbalize a specific audience (e.g., teacher). Strong rereading may be the mechanism by which writers measure text from a reader's perspective without conscious audience commentary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Student vs. professional differences
rubrics_metrics.description: Students display the same activities as professionals but at lower complexity; students were less likely to reread for continuity and tended to look for error more than clarity of meaning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Teaching strategies should target activities that are harder to master (e.g., using lead-writing to develop story direction, editing for revision during writing) and shift lead instruction to be writer-focused rather than solely reader-focused.

rubrics_metrics.name: Coding: underlining (verbalizing while typing)
rubrics_metrics.description: Underlining: writing words said out loud as they are being typed into the text—may not include all words which appear in finished story.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used in protocol transcripts to mark verbalized text that is being produced; helps map spoken/thought activity to written output.

rubrics_metrics.name: Coding 1 — reading/reviewing notes
rubrics_metrics.description: Looking back through parts or all of the information gathered for the story.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identifies moments when writers consult notes as part of planning, recalling, or verifying details.

rubrics_metrics.name: Coding 2 — recalling
rubrics_metrics.description: Remembering information from the news gathering process.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Captures use of memory as a substantive source of content during composition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Coding 3 — analyzing/evaluating
rubrics_metrics.description: Determining meaning, relationships, relevance, importance of information gathered for the story.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Includes assessing which facts or angles fit the developing direction set by the lead.

rubrics_metrics.name: Coding 4 — goal setting
rubrics_metrics.description: Determining desired outcome, determining what needs to be accomplished or what should not be done to all or any part of the task—decisions related to outcomes involving self, meaning, of text itself.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Often expressed as short-term goals for sentences or paragraphs rather than an overall story goal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Coding 5 — planning/organizing
rubrics_metrics.description: Determining strategies to use to meet goals, to carry out desired outcomes, complete the task at hand.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reflects paragraph-level strategy selection and ordering during on-the-spot organization.

rubrics_metrics.name: Coding 6 — translating
rubrics_metrics.description: Determining vocabulary and syntax needed, creating sentences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The moment of language selection and sentence construction from conceptual content.

rubrics_metrics.name: Coding 7 — editing (process)
rubrics_metrics.description: Making changes in written material, adding to, deleting, or replacing written material (during the writing process).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Covers micro-level revisions made as the writer composes and rereads.

rubrics_metrics.name: Coding 8 — reviewing/rereading (process)
rubrics_metrics.description: Rescanning or rereading parts or the whole written text.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used repeatedly during composition to generate next content or check local coherence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Coding 9 — evaluating text
rubrics_metrics.description: Making value statements about the written text or parts of the text, determining worth of written material.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Includes judgments like 'this works' or 'this doesn't' that guide revision decisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Coding 10 — adding new information
rubrics_metrics.description: Drawing on past experiences or knowledge, or drawing on new stories to add information or insight during the writing process.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Represents moments when writers inject new facts, context, analogies, or examples into the developing story.

rubrics_metrics.name: Coding 11 — considering sources
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognition of, judgment of, evaluation of, or consideration of any source or sources of information for the story.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Includes weighing source reliability, deciding whether to include a quote, or recalling source details.

rubrics_metrics.name: Coding 12 — considering audience
rubrics_metrics.description: Referring to any potential reader of the story including editor or staff, sources, or general audience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Captures explicit audience commentary (less frequent among professionals) and who the writer imagines while composing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Final editing (post-composition)
rubrics_metrics.description: Making changes in written material after story is complete.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Part of the process is a final edit for continuity and polish; some writers perform multiple full read-throughs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Full read-through
rubrics_metrics.description: Rereading of entire story.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used as a final check for focus and coherence; often occurs at least once and sometimes multiple times.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interruptions
rubrics_metrics.description: A break in the writing process.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Protocols show interruptions are common but manageable because of localized goals and the lead-provided sense of direction.
